items.title: Focus Question: Why can radio signals from a satellite reach Earth through empty space, and what does that have to do with light?

answer.html: Radio waves and light are both electromagnetic waves: a changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field, which produces a changing electric field, and so on. The two fields regenerate each other, so no material is needed, and the wave crosses a vacuum at 𝑐= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s. Radio waves have a much longer wavelength than visible light but travel the same way.

items.title: Applying Practices: Catching Waves (HS-PS4-5, online): Explain how a Wi-Fi router and a laptop exchange information using electromagnetic waves

answer.html: This is a research and communication task, so it has no single answer. A model response: the router's transmitter drives an oscillating current in its antenna, which sends out a microwave electromagnetic wave whose pulses (digital 1s and 0s) carry the data. The laptop's antenna converts the wave's electric field into an oscillating potential difference, a tuner selects the router's frequency, and the pulses are decoded. Explain these steps with the wave properties from this lesson, including frequency, wavelength (𝜆= 𝑐/ 𝑓), and the way walls absorb or reflect the signal.

check.html: Your communication should name the wave behaviors used (transmission, reflection, absorption, resonance in the tuner).

items.title: Figure 27 (Determine): A 4.0 𝜇F capacitor charged to 12 V is connected to a 0.50 H coil. When the capacitor is fully charged, what is the current? What is the maximum current later in the cycle?

body.html: 𝐶= 4.0 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> F, 𝑉= 12 V, 𝐿= 0.50 H. Unknown: current when the capacitor is fully charged, and the maximum current.

Energy swings between the capacitor's electric field, <sup>12</sup> <sub>𝐶</sub>𝑉<sup>2</sup>, and the coil's magnetic field, <sup>12</sup> <sub>𝐿</sub>𝐼<sup>2</sup>. When the capacitor holds all the energy, no energy is in the coil, so the current is zero. The maximum current occurs when all the energy is in the coil.

answer.html: The current is zero when the capacitor is fully charged. The maximum current is 3.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> A (34 mA), when the capacitor is empty.

check.html: Like a pendulum at the top of its swing (all potential energy, zero speed), and at the bottom (all kinetic energy).

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Cause and Effect (coil-and-capacitor): Describe evidence you could gather to support the claim "When the capacitor voltage is at its maximum, the current in the coil is zero"

answer.html: Connect a voltage probe across the capacitor and a current probe in the circuit, and record both against time with a data logger. The electric energy is <sup>12</sup> <sub>𝐶</sub>𝑉<sup>2</sup> and the magnetic energy is <sup>12</sup>

Evidence supporting the claim would be that every time |𝑉| reaches its peak, the recorded current passes through zero, and when the current is at its peak, 𝑉 is zero, with the sum of the two energies staying nearly constant. You would need the measured 𝑉, 𝐼, and time, and the values of 𝐿 and 𝐶.

check.html: The data should show the same 90° phase shift as a pendulum's position and speed.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Stability and Change (oscillations die out): How would adding a large resistor to a coil-and-capacitor circuit change the oscillations, and how does an amplifier feedback loop keep them going?

answer.html: The resistor converts electrical energy to thermal energy, so the oscillations die out faster (like adding more friction to a pendulum). Some energy also escapes as electromagnetic waves. Feedback from an amplifier supplies stability: a small amplified signal at the circuit's own frequency, in phase with the oscillation, adds back the energy lost each cycle (like timed pushes on a swing). The evidence is that the amplitude stays constant while the amplifier is on and decays when it is off.

check.html: Energy lost per cycle equals energy added per cycle, so the amplitude is steady.

items.title: Get It? (resonant cavity): Why aren't resonant cavities used to produce 100-MHz FM radio waves?

body.html: A resonant cavity's size is comparable to the wavelength, and 𝜆= 𝑐/ 𝑓.

answer.html: The cavity would have to be meters across (the wavelength is 3.0 m), which is impractical. Cavities suit microwaves (centimeter wavelengths). Coil-and-capacitor circuits produce the lower frequencies.

check.html: Lower frequency means longer wavelength, hence a bigger cavity.

items.title: Get It? (antenna direction): Infer why turning a portable radio's telescoping antenna from vertical to horizontal can weaken the reception of a station that transmits with a vertical antenna

answer.html: The wave's electric field accelerates electrons in the receiving antenna along the direction of the field. A vertical transmitting antenna makes a vertical → 𝐸, so the signal is strongest when the receiving rod is vertical (parallel to → 𝐸) and weakest when it is horizontal (perpendicular to → 𝐸).

check.html: This is why antennas are tilted to the best-reception position.

items.title: 46 (Check Your Progress): Explain how sunlight can reach Earth through empty space although sound from the Sun cannot

answer.html: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs matter to pass the vibration along, and there is none between the Sun and Earth. Light is an electromagnetic wave. Accelerating charges in the Sun produce a changing electric field; a changing electric field makes a changing magnetic field, which makes a changing electric field, and so on. The pair of fields regenerates itself and moves outward at the speed of light with → 𝐸 and → 𝐵 perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. No medium is needed.

check.html: This is the Maxwell and Hertz result described in the book.

items.title: 47 (Check Your Progress): Explain why X-rays are used to image bones but radio waves are not, and why radio waves can pass through a wall but visible light cannot

answer.html: X-rays have a very short wavelength and high frequency, so each wave carries enough energy to pass through soft tissue, but bone absorbs more of them, which makes an image; they can also ionize atoms, so exposure is limited. Radio waves have a very long wavelength and low frequency, and they interact only weakly with the wall's atoms, so most of the wave passes through. Visible light is absorbed or reflected by the wall's atoms, so it does not get through. Each part of the spectrum is used where its interaction with matter is useful.

check.html: Matches the book: low-frequency waves mostly heat or pass through; high-frequency waves can ionize.

items.title: 48 (Check Your Progress): Find the frequency of an X-ray with 𝜆= 2.5 × 10−10 m

answer.html: 𝑓= 1.2 × 10<sup>18</sup> Hz (X-ray)

items.title: 49 (Check Your Progress): A car's AM radio uses a vertical rod antenna. What can you deduce about the electric fields in AM radio signals?

answer.html: An antenna responds best when it is parallel to the wave's electric field. Since the rod is vertical, the electric fields of AM signals are (mostly) vertical, meaning the signals are vertically polarized. The magnetic field is then horizontal.

check.html: The transmitting tower is also vertical, and the receiving rod works best when it matches the transmitter's direction.

items.title: 50 (Check Your Progress): A digital audio signal uses 5 V for a 1 and 0 V for a 0. Noise adds up to ±0.5 V. Why is the digital signal less affected by noise than an analog signal?

answer.html: With digital, the receiver only needs to decide whether each pulse is high or low. A 5.0 V pulse with ±0.5 V noise is still read as a 1, and a 0 V pulse with noise as a 0, so the original data is recovered exactly. In an analog signal the exact voltage carries the sound, so the same ±0.5 V noise is added to the sound and cannot be removed. Digital signals can also be stored in computer memory, compressed, and sent long distances.

check.html: The noise is only one tenth of the pulse height, so it cannot flip a bit.

answer.html: Longer. The 2.4-GHz antenna is about 6.3 cm and the 5.8-GHz antenna about 2.6 cm, because lower frequency gives a longer wavelength.

check.html: Frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional.

items.title: Answering the Call: Construct an argument (portable cell tower on a truck versus a satellite phone kit)

question.html: Suppose a town's phone service fails after a flood. Option A: a cell tower on a truck covers a radius of about 5 km, needs fuel, and can be running in 6 hours. Option B: satellite phones are handed out to emergency teams, work anywhere with a clear sky, but each phone serves only one user at a time. (Figures are hypothetical for this exercise.)

answer.html: Claim: the truck tower is better for restoring service to residents, and satellite phones are better for rescue teams. Evidence: the tower covers a wide area (about 𝜋(5 km)<sup>2</sup> ≈80 km<sup>2</sup>) and serves many ordinary phones, while each satellite phone serves one user. Reasoning: a larger coverage per device serves more people sooner, so the tower is better for a whole town. A fair counterargument is that the tower needs 6 hours and fuel, so for the first hours or in a remote area, satellite phones are better. Your own research paper should cite your sources.

check.html: The argument uses evidence from the text and addresses a counterclaim.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon: CER, Explain Your Reasoning (A strong solar storm in 1989 knocked out the power grid in Quebec. Why can a storm in space cause a blackout?)

answer.html: Claim: A solar storm sends charged particles that disturb Earth's magnetic field, and the changing field induces currents in long power lines that overload transformers. Evidence: charged particles feel a force 𝐹= 𝑞𝑣𝐵 in a magnetic field, which makes them follow Earth's field lines (Lesson 3); a changing magnetic field induces an EMF in a conductor, 𝐸𝑀𝐹= 𝐵𝐿𝑣sin𝜃 (Lesson 1); and transformers need a changing flux but are designed for alternating current, so an extra steady induced current can overload them (Lesson 2). Reasoning: the very long power lines act as long wires in a changing field, so a large EMF and current appear in them. This extra current in the transformer windings causes overheating and the grid shuts down. The evidence supports the claim. Complete your own Summary Table and revise your own claim if your evidence calls for it.

check.html: Every step comes from a principle in this module.

items.title: SEP Data Analysis Lab, Claim 1 (a): How should the eyes of aliens that see X-rays of wavelength 1.0 × 10−10 m compare in size with human eyes (visible light about 5.5 × 10−7 m)?

body.html: A detector's size must be comparable to the wavelength it detects, so the eye size scales with the wavelength.
The ratio of wavelengths is
A human eye is about 2.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m across, so the alien eye would be about (2.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m) / (5.5 × 10<sup>3</sup>) = 4.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> m.

answer.html: The aliens' eyes would be about 5500 times smaller than human eyes, only a few micrometers across (smaller than most bacteria), because the size must scale with the wavelength.

check.html: Shorter wavelength means a smaller detector, the opposite of the microwave case where it would be larger.

items.title: SEP Data Analysis Lab, Claim 1 (b): A story says a character wearing a "cloak" that bends all light around her is invisible and can still see out. Is the author correct?

answer.html: No. If all the light bends around her, no light reaches her eyes, so there is nothing for her retina to absorb and she cannot see. If light did reach her eyes and was absorbed, then it would not all be bent around her, and she would be partly visible. Seeing requires light to interact with the eye.

check.html: Seeing requires interaction between light and matter.

items.title: SEP Data Analysis Lab, Claim 1 (c): An inventor claims a transformer in which drawing more current from the secondary makes the primary draw less current. Is this possible?

answer.html: No. For a real transformer, more secondary current means more output power, and this power must come from the primary: Lenz's law makes the secondary current's field oppose the change in the core, so the primary current must increase. A transformer in which the primary current dropped while the output rose would produce more energy than is put in, violating conservation of energy.

check.html: Output power cannot exceed input power, 𝑉<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑠</sub>≤𝑉<sub>𝑝</sub>𝐼<sub>𝑝</sub>.

items.title: Focus Question: What do electric and magnetic fields have to do with light?

answer.html: Light is an electromagnetic wave: a changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field, which produces a changing electric field, and so on. The two fields oscillate at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, and move through space at the speed of light 𝑐= 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m/s. Visible light is a small part of the whole electromagnetic spectrum.

body.html: In an electromagnetic wave, → 𝐸, → 𝐵 and the velocity are mutually perpendicular (Figure 22).

items.title: Figure 27 (Determine): What is the charge on the capacitor when the current is maximum?

answer.html: Zero. When the current is largest, all the energy is stored in the coil's magnetic field (like a pendulum at the bottom of its swing, where all energy is kinetic). So no energy remains in the capacitor's electric field, and the capacitor holds no charge at that instant.

check.html: Energy shifts between the two fields, and total energy stays constant.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Cause and Effect (coil-and-capacitor)

answer.html: The claim to test is that the current determines how the energy is split between the magnetic field (coil) and electric field (capacitor). You could connect a current probe in the circuit and a voltage probe across the capacitor, and record both against time with a data logger. The magnetic energy is <sup>12</sup> <sub>𝐿</sub>𝐼<sup>2</sup> and the electric energy is <sup>12</sup> <sub>𝐶</sub>𝑉<sup>2</sup>. Evidence would be that when |𝐼| is at a maximum, 𝑉 across the capacitor is zero, and when 𝐼 is zero, 𝑉 is at a maximum, with the sum of the two energies staying constant (apart from small losses). You would need to measure current, capacitor potential difference, and time, and know 𝐿 and 𝐶.

check.html: The measurements should show the same 90° phase shift between current and capacitor voltage as the pendulum's speed and height.

items.title: Crosscutting Concepts: Stability and Change (oscillations die out)

answer.html: The oscillations fade because energy leaves the circuit: some is carried off as electromagnetic waves, and some is converted to thermal energy by the circuit's resistance (just as friction stops a pendulum). Adding a transformer provides stability: the oscillating current is sent to an amplifier whose output goes to the coil of the transformer, which adds energy back to the circuit at the same frequency and in phase (resonance, like timed pushes on a swing). The evidence is that the amplified current has the same frequency as the coil-and-capacitor circuit, so each push adds energy rather than disrupting the oscillations, keeping the amplitude steady.

check.html: Without the added energy, the amplitude decays; with it, the amplitude is constant.

items.title: Get It? (resonant cavity): Why can't resonant cavities be used to produce infrared waves?

answer.html: A resonant cavity's size sets the frequency, so for frequencies above about 100 GHz the cavity would have to be as small as a molecule, which is impossible to build. Infrared waves come from vibrating nuclei in molecules instead.

check.html: Infrared frequencies are far above the 0.4 to 100 GHz microwave range of cavities.

items.title: Get It? (antenna direction): Infer why the direction in which an antenna points affects its function

answer.html: The wave's electric field accelerates electrons in the antenna along the direction of the field (the wave's polarization). The effect is largest when the antenna is parallel to → 𝐸 and zero when it is perpendicular, so an antenna must point so that it is aligned with the wave's polarization to get the largest signal.

check.html: This is why a rod antenna is tilted until the picture or sound is clearest.

items.title: 46 (Check Your Progress): Explain how electromagnetic waves propagate through space

answer.html: An accelerating charge (such as electrons driven back and forth in an antenna) makes a changing electric field. A changing electric field produces a changing magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field in turn produces a changing electric field. This coupled pair of fields regenerates itself and moves outward at the speed of light, with
𝐸 and
𝐵 perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel. No medium is needed, so the wave can cross a vacuum.

check.html: This is the Maxwell and Hertz result described in the book.

items.title: 47 (Check Your Progress): How do different wavelengths interact with matter, and how does this affect how we use them?

answer.html: Lower-frequency, longer waves (radio, microwave, infrared) are mostly absorbed and converted to thermal energy or pass through, or reflect off ionized layers: radio carries broadcasts, microwaves cook food by heating its water and fat, and infrared is used for heat sensing and night vision. Visible light is detected by eyes. Higher-frequency, shorter waves (UV, X-rays, gamma rays) carry enough energy per photon to ionize atoms and break molecules, which damages living cells: UV causes sunburn and is used to sterilize, X-rays pass through soft tissue but are stopped by bone, which makes images, and X-rays and gamma rays are used to destroy cancer cells. So we use each part of the spectrum where its interaction with matter is useful, and we protect ourselves against the high-frequency end.

check.html: Matches Figure 24: low-frequency absorption gives heating, high-frequency absorption gives ionization.

answer.html: 𝑓= 2.0 × 10<sup>13</sup> Hz (infrared)

check.html: Infrared range in Figure 23.

items.title: 49 (Check Your Progress): Radio antennas have horizontal rods. What can you deduce about the electric fields in radio signals?

answer.html: An antenna responds best when it is parallel to the wave's electric field. Since the rods are horizontal, the electric fields of the radio signals are (mostly) horizontal, meaning the signals are horizontally polarized. The magnetic field is then vertical.

check.html: An electromagnetic wave from an antenna has → 𝐸 parallel to the antenna, so receiving rods matching the transmitter's direction work best.

items.title: 50 (Check Your Progress): Advantages of storing and transmitting information digitally

answer.html: Digital signals can send more information in the same amount of time than AM or FM, are less affected by noise (only 1s and 0s must be told apart, not an exact amplitude), can be stored reliably in computer memory, and can be sent long distances and compressed (digital TV fits four or more channels in the space of one analog channel).

check.html: These are the advantages listed in the text.

body.html: The most efficient antenna is half a wavelength long. 𝜆= 𝑐/ 𝑓, so lower frequency means longer wavelength.

answer.html: Longer. The 88-MHz antenna is about 1.7 m (half-wave) and the 108-MHz antenna about 1.4 m, because lower frequency gives a longer wavelength.

check.html: Frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional.

items.title: 53 (Check Your Progress, Critical Thinking): Why are scientists concerned about the thinning ozone layer?

answer.html: UV radiation has a higher frequency and shorter wavelength than visible light, so each wave carries more energy and can ionize atoms and molecules and cause chemical reactions. Ozone absorbs most of the Sun's UV. If the layer thins, more UV reaches the surface, increasing harm such as sunburn, skin cancer, cataracts, damage to DNA in living cells, and damage to plants and plankton.

check.html: The book says short-wavelength radiation can ionize atoms and damage living cells.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon: CER, Explain Your Reasoning (Northern Lights)

answer.html: Claim: The Northern Lights are caused by charged particles from the Sun that follow Earth's magnetic field lines to the polar regions and excite atoms in the upper atmosphere, which emit light. Evidence: a magnetic field exerts a force 𝐹= 𝑞𝑣𝐵 perpendicular to the velocity of a charged particle, giving circular or spiral paths with 𝑟= 𝑚𝑣/ (𝑞𝐵) (Lesson 3); electromagnetic waves, including visible light, are produced by accelerating charges and by energy changes in atoms (Lesson 4); and the green light's wavelength (525 nm) is within the visible spectrum. Reasoning: because the field guides the charged particles, they arrive near the poles, where they collide with atmospheric atoms. The atoms release the energy as light, so the evidence supports the claim. Complete your own Summary Table and revise your own claim if your evidence calls for it.

check.html: Every step in the argument comes from a principle in this module.

items.title: SEP Data Analysis Lab, Claim 1 (a): How should the aliens' eyes compare in size to human eyes? (Microwave-sensitive eyes)

body.html: To form a sharp image, an eye's opening (and detector) must be much larger than the wavelength it detects, and antennas work best when about half a wavelength long. Microwaves have wavelengths of about 1 cm to 30 cm compared with about 5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup> m for visible light.
The ratio of wavelengths is

<sub>5.5</sub><sub> ×</sub><sub> 10</sub><sup>−</sup><sup>7</sup><sup> </sup><sub>m</sub> ≈1.8 × 10<sup>4</sup>. To work as well as a human eye, the alien eye would need to be tens of thousands of times larger than a human eye if the wavelength is 1 cm, and even larger for longer microwaves.

answer.html: The aliens' eyes would have to be enormously larger than human eyes: on the order of 10<sup>4</sup> times larger (hundreds of meters across) to see microwaves as sharply as we see light, because the size must scale with the wavelength.

check.html: This is a scaling argument; the exact factor depends on which microwave wavelength they see.

items.title: SEP Data Analysis Lab, Claim 1 (b): Is Wells correct that the invisible man can see?

answer.html: No. To be invisible, light must pass through his body and eyes without being absorbed, reflected, or refracted. But to see, the eye must absorb light in the retina to produce a signal. If his retina absorbed the light, it would be visible (a dark spot); if it did not absorb light, he could not detect it. So an invisible person would be blind.

check.html: Seeing requires interaction between light and matter.

items.title: SEP Data Analysis Lab, Claim 1 (c): Is the "anti-Lenz's law" possible?

answer.html: No. In real systems Lenz's law makes the induced current oppose the change that caused it, so more electrical output requires more mechanical effort. An "anti-Lenz's law" would make the generator easier to turn as more energy is drawn out, producing more electrical energy than the mechanical work put in. That violates conservation of energy and amounts to a perpetual motion machine.

check.html: The book says the opposing force on a generator is "consistent with the law of conservation of energy."
